extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners referencing USPTO guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether claims satisfy 35 U.S.C. §101 subject-matter eligibility (including treatment of living subject matter, BRI, Alice/Mayo two-part test, and the four statutory categories). Intended to direct examiners through Step 1 (statutory categories) and Step 2 (judicial exceptions) and the eligibility flowchart (Pathways A/B/C).

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct inventorship requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The application must set forth the correct inventorship; failure to do so can lead to rejections under applicable statutory provisions (e.g., 35 U.S.C. 101 and 115, and pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(f) for pre-AIA applications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §2137.01 for detailed inventorship discussion and MPEP §602.01(c) et seq. for correction of inventorship. Use appropriate form paragraphs (e.g., see MPEP §706.03(a), subsection IV) when rejecting for failure to set forth correct inventorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two criteria for subject matter eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: To be eligible under 35 U.S.C. 101, a claimed invention must (a) fall within one of the four statutory categories (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter), and (b) be directed to patent-eligible subject matter and not to a judicial exception unless the claim as a whole includes additional limitations amounting to significantly more than the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §2106 for detailed discussion. Both criteria must be evaluated (Step 1 addresses the statutory categories; Step 2 applies the Alice/Mayo framework to identify judicial exceptions and determine whether additional limitations provide 'significantly more').

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility requirement (specific, substantial, credible)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention must be useful; the utility must be specific, substantial, and credible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §2107 for a detailed discussion of utility. Utility is distinct from eligibility under §101 (i.e., utility is not the test for patent-eligible subject matter), but it is a separate statutory requirement that must be satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human organisms excluded from patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to or encompassing a human organism are nonstatutory and cannot be patented pursuant to AIA sec. 33(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim as a whole encompasses a human organism, make a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 and AIA sec. 33(a) indicating the claim is directed to a human organism and therefore nonstatutory. Use form paragraph 7.04.03 and continue to examine other patentability issues (35 U.S.C. 102/103/112) as applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1 — Four statutory categories (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim as a whole is directed to a process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter. For product categories (machine, manufacture, composition) the subject matter generally must have a physical or tangible form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions and examples: 'process' = series of acts or steps; 'machine' = concrete thing consisting of parts or combination of devices; 'manufacture' = tangible article given new form/quality/property by human activity; 'composition of matter' = combination of two or more substances. See MPEP §2106.03 for citations and examples. It is sufficient if the claim falls into at least one category; it need not be assigned a single 'correct' category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-statutory examples for Step 1
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain claimed subject matter does not fall within the four statutory categories (and so fails Step 1), including information/data per se, a computer program per se (software per se) claimed as a product without structural recitations, transitory signal transmissions (carrier waves), and subject matter expressly prohibited (e.g., humans per se).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-limiting examples: data per se; software per se when claimed as a product without structure; signals per se (propagating electrical/electromagnetic signals); transitory carrier waves. Use Federal Circuit precedent (e.g., Digitech, Nuijten, Mentor Graphics) when assessing whether a claim covers non-statutory embodiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: BRI must be established before eligibility analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim as a whole prior to evaluating eligibility; the BRI sets claim boundaries and affects whether the claim covers statutory or non-statutory subject matter and whether it is directed to a judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluating eligibility under the BRI prevents the outcome from depending on the drafter's art. Claim interpretation can affect both Step 1 (e.g., whether a medium encompasses non-statutory carrier waves) and Step 2 (e.g., whether claim limitations require computer implementation, or amount to an improvement in technology). See MPEP §2111 for BRI guidance and cases such as Mentor Graphics, Enfish, Synopsys, McRO, and Amdocs for examples of how construction affects eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2 — Alice/Mayo two-part test (determine judicial exception and inventive concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the Alice/Mayo framework: Step 2A — determine whether the claims are directed to a judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon); Step 2B — if so, determine whether the claim recites additional elements (individually or in combination) that amount to significantly more than the exception (i.e., an 'inventive concept' or practical application).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Alice/Mayo test (Mayo/Alice) is the only test that should be used to evaluate eligibility under Step 2. If claims are directed to an exception, search for an 'inventive concept' beyond the judicial exception. The machine-or-transformation test and other superseded tests (e.g., 'useful, concrete and tangible result' or 'special purpose computer') may be considered as clues but are not separate tests for eligibility. See MPEP §§2106.04 and 2106.05 for detailed guidance and Supreme Court/Federal Circuit precedent (Alice, Mayo, Bilski, Diehr, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine-or-transformation and other older tests are only clues
rubrics_metrics.description: The machine-or-transformation test and other older tests (e.g., 'useful, concrete, and tangible result', 'special purpose computer') are not separate eligibility tests but can serve as considerations in the 'significantly more' inquiry under Alice/Mayo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use machine-or-transformation as part of the Step 2B analysis (a clue toward 'significantly more') but do not apply it as an independent test. Recognize that certain Federal Circuit rationales like In re Alappat have been superseded by Bilski and Alice; mere recitation of concrete components is insufficient to confer eligibility on an otherwise abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility flowchart — Pathways A, B, and C
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the eligibility flowchart: Pathway A (streamlined analysis) — claims that fall within a statutory category and whose eligibility is self-evident; Pathway B — claims that fall within a statutory category and are not directed to a judicial exception (no Step 2B required); Pathway C — claims that fall within a statutory category, are directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A YES), but recite additional elements that amount to significantly more (Step 2B YES).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If uncertain whether streamlined analysis (Pathway A) applies, conduct the full eligibility analysis. If a claim is not eligible under any pathway, reject under 35 U.S.C. 101. Regardless of a 101 rejection, continue complete examination under 35 U.S.C. 102, 103, and 112 as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: BRI covering both statutory and non-statutory embodiments requires rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: If the broadest reasonable interpretation of a claim covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments, the claim embraces non-eligible subject matter and fails Step 1 (should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When this occurs, best practice is to point out the BRI and recommend an amendment that narrows the claim to statutory embodiments if possible. Example: claims to 'machine-readable medium' that encompass both RAM (statutory) and carrier waves (non-statutory) should be rejected and applicant advised to amend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Living subject matter — 'markedly different characteristics' analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Living subject matter can be patent-eligible where it is not a 'product of nature' and possesses 'markedly different characteristics from any found in nature' (Chakrabarty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the 'markedly different characteristics' analysis to determine whether a nature-based product (including living matter) is eligible. See MPEP §2106.04(b) and §2106.04(c) and relevant case law (Chakrabarty, Myriad, Roslin). Be aware that mere cloning or exact genetic replicas (e.g., Dolly in Roslin) that do not possess markedly different characteristics may be ineligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: §101 is a threshold inquiry; continue full examination under other statutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent-eligibility under §101 is only a threshold test; even if claims satisfy §101, they must still meet the other requirements of the Patent Act (novelty under §102, nonobviousness under §103, and adequate disclosure under §112, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should make a complete examination of every claim for 35 U.S.C. 102, 103, and 112, as well as utility, inventorship, double patenting, and any non-statutory double patenting issues. See the Bilski quote and MPEP §2103.
